items.title: Jon Weber interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 2, 2012
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] ...we can tell stories about like Bix Beiderbecke, of course, he’ll live on forever partly because he died so young.

ctx.x: Yeah. I was glad. If I hadn’t encountered that who knows, maybe I would have followed a different route. I’ve still never smoked marijuana my entire life, what kind of a musician am I? And I don’t drink. Although you will probably observe younger musicians — I’m 51 — people younger than me are, the next generation of musicians are the healthiest bunch of people. You know? I mean in Duke’s day at three in the morning, “Let’s go get a steak and a bottle of champagne and some heroin” or whatever. I’m kidding. But I…

I think sometimes the audience in the older days liked the fact that those musicians were going to die young. It’s like let them be that way so we can watch. You know, or then we can tell stories about like Bix Beiderbecke, of course, he’ll live on forever partly because he died so young. And the tragic hero I suppose.

There is the mystique of the dark side, the flirtation with the vice that jazz brings — all the best jazz photography is black and white, smoky club basements, sweaty and guys going “yeah, yeah.” You know there’s this whole feeling of sort of nocturnal and nefarious and sort of, oh — and even here I’m the most substance-free musician there is, but I like going out to a place at three in the morning because there’s something about that life, something about that energy that really attracts me and attracts a lot of…
